files.why: The Choices class (and its subclasses IntegerChoices, TextChoices) lack the do_not_call_in_templates flag. This causes the template engine to call them with no arguments, breaking template comparisons like {% if student.year_in_school == YearInSchool.FRESHMAN %}.

steps.change: Add the attribute `do_not_call_in_templates = True` as a class attribute on the Choices class (after the __str__ method, at the same indentation level — a clear, idiomatic location consistent with how related_descriptors.py uses it).
steps.expected: Choices and all its subclasses (IntegerChoices, TextChoices, and any user-defined enum) will have do_not_call_in_templates = True, so the template engine will skip calling them (line 852 of base.py: `if getattr(current, 'do_not_call_in_templates', False): pass`). Enum classes will resolve to themselves in templates, allowing dotted attribute access to enum members like FRESHMAN.

plan_json.completeness_check: I verified that only enums.py needs changing: (1) the template engine check at django/template/base.py:851-852 is the only place that reads do_not_call_in_templates — no other template code needs updating; (2) no other Django code consumes or guards Choices in a way that would need a corollary change; (3) the pattern is exactly how related_descriptors.py and contenttypes/fields.py already solve the same problem for their callable classes.

files.why: This file contains the `in_bulk()` method which raises `ValueError` when `field_name` does not correspond to a field with `unique=True`. The check must also accept single-field total `UniqueConstraint`s (those without a condition).

steps.change: Replace the condition `not self.model._meta.get_field(field_name).unique` with `not self.model._meta.get_field(field_name).unique and not any(field_name in constraint.fields for constraint in self.model._meta.total_unique_constraints())`
steps.expected: The `in_bulk()` method no longer raises `ValueError` when `field_name` is covered by a single-field `UniqueConstraint` without a condition. The existing check for `field.unique` is preserved, and the new check uses the existing `Options.total_unique_constraints()` helper (which already filters out constraints with a condition). Only total unique constraints (no condition) are considered because partial constraints do not guarantee row-level uniqueness for all rows.

plan_json.completeness_check: Only one location in the Django source checks `field.unique` to guard `in_bulk()` — line 692 of `django/db/models/query.py`. The `Options.total_unique_constraints()` helper already exists and returns exactly the set of constraints we need (unconditional unique constraints). No other files call `in_bulk` internally within Django's own code, and no other validation gates reject non-`unique=True` fields for this method. Therefore the single-file fix is complete.

files.why: AuthenticationForm.__init__ sets self.fields['username'].max_length after field init, but never updates the widget's HTML attrs with the maxlength attribute.

steps.expected: After the change, when AuthenticationForm is rendered, the username <input> element will include the maxlength HTML attribute (e.g., maxlength="254"), matching the behavior before the regression.

plan_json.completeness_check: Only one file needs changing: the bug is entirely in AuthenticationForm.__init__ setting max_length on the field but not the widget. UsernameField.widget_attrs correctly delegates to CharField.widget_attrs, and CharField.widget_attrs already has the logic to set maxlength — it just wasn't called at the right time. No other call sites or consumers need modification because the widget's attrs dict is the single source of truth for HTML rendering, and no other field has this deferred max_length pattern.

files.why: The `check_uri()` function performs a GET request when checking anchors but never validates the HTTP response status code, so HTTP errors like 404 are masked as 'Anchor not found'.

steps.target: sphinx/builders/linkcheck.py : check_uri() — the `if anchor and self.app.config.linkcheck_anchors:` branch (lines 164–172)
steps.change: After the `requests.get()` call on line 167-168 and before the `found = check_anchor(...)` call on line 169, insert `response.raise_for_status()` to raise an `HTTPError` if the server returned a non-2xx status. This follows the same pattern already used in the `else` branch (lines 179 and 185).
steps.expected: When the anchor-checking branch receives a response with an HTTP error status (e.g. 404), `raise_for_status()` raises `HTTPError`, which is caught by the existing `except HTTPError as err:` handler on line 186, returning `('broken', str(err), 0)` — i.e. the real HTTP error message instead of 'Anchor not found'.

plan_json.completeness_check: Only `sphinx/builders/linkcheck.py` needs changing. The `check_anchor()` function (called on line 169) is correct as-is — it just parses HTML; the bug is that it is called without first checking the HTTP response status. The `except` clauses on lines 186–199 already handle `HTTPError` and generic `Exception` correctly, so the single insertion of `response.raise_for_status()` after the GET request is sufficient and consistent with the existing code in the same function's `else` branch (lines 179 and 185). No other file calls, extends, or guards this logic.

files.why: This file contains the HEAD-then-GET fallback logic for link checking. The inner `except HTTPError:` clause (line 175) only catches `HTTPError`, but `TooManyRedirects` is a sibling subclass of `RequestException`, not a subclass of `HTTPError`. So when `requests.head()` raises `TooManyRedirects`, it bypasses the GET fallback and gets caught by the outer `except Exception` handler (line 190), marking the link as broken even though a GET request might succeed.

steps.change: Add `TooManyRedirects` to the existing import from `requests.exceptions`, changing line 23 from `from requests.exceptions import HTTPError` to `from requests.exceptions import HTTPError, TooManyRedirects`.
steps.expected: `TooManyRedirects` is now available as a name in the module scope for use in exception handlers.

steps.change: Change the bare `except HTTPError:` on line 175 to `except (HTTPError, TooManyRedirects):` so that `TooManyRedirects` exceptions raised by the HEAD request also trigger the GET fallback.
steps.expected: When `requests.head()` raises `TooManyRedirects`, the code now falls back to `requests.get()` (lines 178-180) instead of propagating the exception to outer handlers that mark the link as broken.

plan_json.completeness_check: I verified that the only HEAD request call with fallback logic is in `check_uri()` in `sphinx/builders/linkcheck.py`. The `sphinx.util.requests.head()` wrapper is a thin pass-through that does not implement its own fallback — it just delegates to `requests.head()`. No other file in the repo performs a HEAD-then-GET fallback, so this single-file change is complete.

files.why: Contains the __init_subclass__ logic that builds the `parent_links` dict (lines 194-207). When multiple OneToOneFields point to the same parent model, the last one processed overwrites the earlier one. If a non-parent-link field is defined after a parent-link field, the wrong field is stored and later causes ImproperlyConfigured in options.py.

steps.change: Modify the inner loop body to only overwrite an existing parent_links entry for a given key if the incoming field has `parent_link=True`. Change from unconditionally assigning `parent_links[make_model_tuple(related)] = field` to: compute the key, then set it only if the key is absent or the new field has `parent_link=True`.
steps.expected: When multiple OneToOneFields target the same model, the one with `parent_link=True` is always stored in `parent_links`, regardless of field definition order. This means `parent_links[{Document_key}]` correctly stores `document_ptr` (with parent_link=True) instead of `origin` (without parent_link=True).

plan_json.completeness_check: I checked all call sites that consume `self.parents` or `parent_links`: options.py (lines 241-257 for PK setup, line 626 for get_ancestor_link), base.py (line 572 for _set_pk_val), deletion.py (lines 190, 254 for cascade logic). All of these just use whatever field is stored in `self.parents`; none independently re-derive which field has parent_link. The only place that decides which field goes into `self.parents` is the `parent_links` dict in base.py. No system checks or validators touch parent_link. So fixing the single loop in base.py is complete.

files.why: Contains `PyMethod.get_index_text()` which generates index entries with spurious parens when the `:property:` option is used. This is the only file that participates in generating index text for `py:method` directives.

steps.change: Change `_('%s() (%s property)')` to `_('%s (%s property)')` — remove the empty parentheses `()` after the method name in the property branch of the index text.
steps.expected: When `py:method` is used with `:property:`, the index entry for a qualified name (e.g. `Foo.bar`) will read `bar (Foo property)` instead of `bar() (Foo property)`.

steps.change: In the `except ValueError` branch (handles unqualified names without a dot), add a guard `if 'property' in self.options:` that returns the name without trailing `()`. Return `_('%s (in module %s)') % (name, modname)` when a module is present, or plain `name` otherwise. The existing `%s()` paths remain for the non-property cases.
